The day's discussion centered on **Kimi K3**, Moonshot's newly API-available open model, framed by many as a [possible 'DeepSeek moment'](/?date=2026-07-17&category=social#item-65b3961dae66).

- **Simon Willison** [posted detailed notes](/?date=2026-07-17&category=social#item-58eb61beea98) on **Kimi K3** and reflected on what his pelican SVG benchmark still reveals about frontier models.
- **Ethan Mollick** [gave a firsthand caution](/?date=2026-07-17&category=social#item-c160a3619521) that **Kimi K3 Max** made repeated statistical errors auditing his academic work, tempering launch hype.
- Open-model researchers [celebrated broad momentum](/?date=2026-07-17&category=social#item-38c0e48df4ea) across **K3, GLM 5.2, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and Inkling**, arguing ['distillation' excuses should end](/?date=2026-07-17&category=social#item-4183084776e4) and that China now builds genuinely excellent models.

Infrastructure and forecasting milestones drew technical attention.
- The **vLLM** team unpacked **KV cache management** as [one of inference's hardest problems](/?date=2026-07-17&category=social#item-ee7d180271c3) and [touted day-0 Kimi K3 support](/?date=2026-07-17&category=social#item-4badfe01bee5).
- The **Forecasting Research Institute** [reported several AI systems](/?date=2026-07-17&category=social#item-8dc0e982eff3) are now statistically indistinguishable from human superforecasters.

Leadership and research rounded out the pulse.
- **Sam Altman** [admitted OpenAI's uneven year](/?date=2026-07-17&category=social#item-83efc8264242) while pledging its best 12 months ahead, and said he now [talks to ChatGPT more than he types](/?date=2026-07-17&category=social#item-4058b882c8b2).
- **Simon Willison** [dissected the open-sourced](/?date=2026-07-17&category=social#item-ae3982ea09db) **Grok Build CLI** (~844k lines of Rust); **Yann LeCun** [argued inductive bias and regularization](/?date=2026-07-17&category=social#item-190a75847f8f) underlie all generalization; **Google DeepMind** [announced a bioresilience partnership](/?date=2026-07-17&category=social#item-9939514b3583) with **Isomorphic Labs**.

items.title: @GoogleResearch Not a critique of the paper, but isn't inductive bias/ regularization the reason for...
items.author: @ylecun
items.summary: LeCun argues that inductive bias and regularization underlie every form of generalization, noting weight magnitude limits make functions Lipschitz and yield smoother score functions.
items.reasoning: Technically deep observation from a top researcher engaging with a Google Research paper, with strong engagement.
items.summary_html: LeCun argues that inductive bias and regularization underlie every form of generalization, noting weight magnitude limits make functions Lipschitz and yield smoother score functions.
items.content_html:
@GoogleResearch Not a critique of the paper, but isn't inductive bias/ regularization the reason for *every* form of generalization?

Neural nets have a number of inductive biases due to the architecture as well as explicit or implicit regularizations.

The mere fact that weight magnitudes are limited (e.g. through regularization) makes the input-output function Lipschitz, which is the property you want to produce a smooth score function.

Grateful for the shoutout and collab. The...
items.content:
Congrats to @Kimi_Moonshot on the Kimi K3 announcement! 🎉

Grateful for the shoutout and collab. The Kimi team announced they contributed a KDA prefix caching implementation directly to vLLM, to be released alongside the model. 🚀

KDA breaks assumptions behind conventional prefix caching, and this upstream work means the community gets efficient long-context serving from day 0.

vLLM will support Kimi K3 on day-0 release.

Open weights by July 27, 2026.

items.title: Modern language models can accept very long inputs, but it remains unclear whether they can reliably...
items.content:
Modern language models can accept very long inputs, but it remains unclear whether they can reliably find one useful document among thousands without relying on a separate search model that represents queries and documents as vectors and compares their similarity. 

This paper from UCB and UT Austin tests that possibility with corpora approaching one million tokens and with input lengths far beyond those used during training.

The authors develop a 0.6-billion-parameter model called BlockSearch, then trace its failure at large scales to "attention dilution:" the transformer often assigns the relevant document a strong raw score, but the scores from many irrelevant documents accumulate when those scores are converted into attention weights, weakening the useful signal.

They test two focused remedies—adjusting this conversion according to corpus size and letting later layers examine only a shortlist of documents—and recover performance close to a strong vector-based search model on standard benchmarks.

On a separate task where relevance depends on exact wording rather than broad semantic similarity, their best version performs several times better than the vector-based baseline, while still declining as the corpus grows.

https://t.co/y3EbrMWDoT

items.title:
what does it really mean to "own your intelligence"?

1. can the system compound *on your terms*? th...
items.content:
what does it really mean to "own your intelligence"?

1. can the system compound *on your terms*? the durable advantage is not the model/system at this point in time - it's the flywheel that compounds over time

2. intelligence is no longer just the model - its the system around the model. if the system is opaque or locked away, you are renting intelligence (not owning it)

3. own the harness. integrate it deeply into your systems. make it specific to the task at hand

4. own the context and memory layer. includes user preferences, org knowledge, workflow patterns. if memory is trapped in vendor product, your learning is trapped to

5. own model optionality. you need freedom to route across models, providers, deployment modes. different tasks require different tradeoffs

6. own the economics. intelligence only matters if you can afford to deploy it broadly. sustainable intelligence at scale

7. own the feedback loop. observability tells you what happened, evals tell you if it worked. without this loop you cannot measure the intelligence, you are guessing

s/o @nlarusstone @nfcampos for their thoughts on feedback

I do think that for any given task, you can always distill a generalized model/agent harness into a specialized model/harness/workflow for higher accuracy and lower cost.

The more narrow the data and task domain, the more opportunity there is to optimize performance (not to mention provide a more targeted UX vs. a chat interface). 

As agents get better at improving themselves, I think you can start to perform this distillation automatically, by defining a top-level goal and evaluation rubric, instead of codifying the workflow through code or natural language.

items.title: Generating every intermediate reasoning step as text makes language models slow, while earlier attem...
items.content:
Generating every intermediate reasoning step as text makes language models slow, while earlier attempts to keep those steps inside the model’s hidden states tended to lose accuracy as models grew.

This paper presents LOTUS, which gives a transformer several hidden "workspaces," repeatedly processes them with the same network layers, and trains each workspace to correspond to a known reasoning step; the hidden computation can therefore proceed largely in parallel rather than one token at a time.

On a 3-billion-parameter model, it comes close to ordinary chain-of-thought accuracy on math problems while reducing reasoning latency by about 2.5 times for compact calculations and 6.9 times for longer verbal solutions, and its hidden states can often be decoded into meaningful intermediate steps rather than remaining entirely opaque.

This is smart: it's the first LM architecture I heard of that contains parts designed specifically to represent reasoning steps.

https://t.co/J7ydkp6i7u

items.content:
Great work from the LightSeek team on TokenSpeed's day-0 Inkling support. Their new KV cache manager—a single flat paged pool with heterogeneous views—fits full, sliding-window, and convolution states into one allocator without padding or fragmentation.

That's the same principle behind Jenga (https://t.co/Zd7OzzQ4sZ): separate physical memory allocation from logical organization. 

Great to see the ecosystem converging here as attention patterns keep diversifying; thanks to the LightSeek team for the acknowledgment!

Great work from the LightSeek team on TokenSpeed's day-0 Inkling support. Their new KV cache manager—a single flat paged pool with heterogeneous views—fits full, sliding-window, and convolution states into one allocator without padding or fragmentation.

That's the same principle behind Jenga (https://t.co/Zd7OzzQ4sZ): separate physical memory allocation from logical organization.

Great to see the ecosystem converging here as attention patterns keep diversifying; thanks to the LightSeek team for the acknowledgment!

items.title: I had dinner with @bercankilic a few months ago. He collects, and prepares, data to build world mode...
items.content:
I had dinner with @bercankilic a few months ago. He collects, and prepares, data to build world models for robotics. 

And he is very good at it. Probably because he worked on Formula 1 cars collecting data (he told me the team he worked at had a couple of petabytes of data from one car). 

Bercan is very interesting, because he is one of a few people building the future of robotics. If you really want to know where robots are, he's one who really knows (and meeting many of them is why I believe it will be at least a year or two before humanoids will be generalized, and could take a few more years to get really useful for a wide range of people and businesses, which is why I wrote that Tesla's Optimus will probably slip into next year before Elon reveals it for purchase).

items.title: The number of posts praising the new thinky machines model which you wouldn't prefer over any other ...
items.content:
The number of posts praising the new thinky machines model which you wouldn't prefer over any other model for any task and the aggressiveness of the comments under my post shows where the billions actually went.

The excuses that the model isn't stronger because look how many modalities it supports is ridiculous. In 2026, data of additional modalities is supposed to make the model stronger not weaker.

One clown went even further saying that it's the best open-weight model "outside of China" as if the geography could be an excuse for the lack of any competitive advantage.

Others just praise that fact that the model is open weight as if hugging face wasn't drowning in mediocre open weight models no one ever downloads.

If tomorrow a noname lab released such a model everyone would have yawned and kept scrolling.

Key caveats:

• We last elicited superforecaster predictions in 2024. Our comparison relies on a statistical extrapolation that grows less reliable over time.

• Results depend on realized questions and are inherently stochastic. As more questions resolve, the results may shift.

• The 95% CIs for many of these submissions overlap substantially; the results are more consistent with superforecaster parity than with outperformance.

• These findings don't mean that ForecastBench is saturated. The superforecaster median is a human reference point, and it is possible that AI systems may exceed superforecaster accuracy.

items.title:
You can now test 100 AI-written harness changes unattended. Seven survived.

@zhengyaojiang reports ...
items.content:
You can now test 100 AI-written harness changes unattended. Seven survived.

@zhengyaojiang reports one system rewrote his company's own harness across eight days, using an external benchmark to decide what stayed.

That sounds like recursive self-improvement. But did the surviving changes cause the gain?

> A model proposes the change
> The harness rewrites itself
> Scored on an external benchmark
> Winners become the next starting point

One result should make engineers pause: neutral code received credit in about 60% of one-run comparisons.

At that point, the demo becomes a release-engineering problem. A higher score is not enough if the mechanism never fired, the gain disappears across seeds, or ordinary retries do better.

We traced what the evidence proves, where it breaks, and what a team should demand before shipping a self-improving harness.

Full article in the first reply ↓↓

How to monitor the web and research what comes back in 300 lines of code.

I want to buy some cheap ...
items.content:
How to monitor the web and research what comes back in 300 lines of code.

I want to buy some cheap products on Amazon, but I want to grab them when prices drop.

I'm using Parallel @p0 here, which is a really easy way to ground your agentic code.

Here is how this works:

1. Set up a monitoring event with Parallel for the products
2. If there's a hit, I get a webhook event with the details
3. My script immediately kicks off a Deep Research task
4. The final result tells me whether the product is worth buying

I probably spent 1 hour building all of this with Claude Code + the Parallel Agent Skills. I'm linking to the GitHub repo below.

Just think about what you could do with this. Here is an easy example (I also set this up):

• Monitor news for public tech companies
• Analyze the news + price
• Assess whether it's worth investing

You can do this, put it on autopilot, and get an email anytime there's something worth your time.

Here is the video I recorded.

items.title:
I was still in high school when this was recorded.

But back then there was no X. No Facebook. No Yo...
items.content:
I was still in high school when this was recorded.

But back then there was no X. No Facebook. No YouTube. No TikTok. No Instagram. 

So no one saw it back then. Including me, and I was Apple's first fan (having made Apple II mother boards in our house back in 1978). 

So even I didn't realize just how far ahead Jobs was. 

When I met Steve Wozniak in 1989 no one recognized him. We sat in West Valley Community College's cafeteria every morning with hundreds of people walking past. Only about five people in a semester ever figured out Apple's cofounder was sitting in the cafeteria. 

Today we live in a different world. Which is one reason why the world is speeding up. I have lists of about 50,000 here who are working in AI in some way. 

You can learn faster today about what's happening on the bleeding edge than you could back then. 

I notice that even in 1983 almost no one had a personal computer. 

We are there with a range of things today. How many have had even a ride in ANY autonomous car? Only a few million out of eight billion people. 

How many have worn a brain/computer interface? Even fewer. 

How many have used a Quantum computer? Even fewer. 

How many have built an AI agent from scratch? A few million. 

How many have met a humanoid robot? Fewer. 

How many have experienced an Apple Vision Pro? A few million. 

I got ahead of Steve once, when Siri was launched in my house. He caught on very quickly once it was publicly disclosed. Bought the company within the first month or so of it being out. 

The leaders we all see just change so freaking quickly. It usually takes me a lot longer to change. I saw this while walking around with Mark Zuckerberg. We talked about FriendFeed and within a month he had bought it. 

One thing that most of the industry still hasn't caught up to Jobs on was his ability to explain complex things simply. 

I was blessed to hear him talk a couple of times and once I noticed that every sentence that came out of his mouth could be turned into a Tweet. Back then we were limited to short posts (about 1/10th as long as this one). 

Every sentence he said could be grabbed and made into a post. 

A skill I don't have, although I try. And I've sat through thousands of company pitches since then and so few people have that skill. 

Another difference? Back then there were only a few dozen companies building for personal computers. Now my lists here on X have 9,000 AI companies. 

Welcome to the new world.

Agents don't just respond. They reason, write code, query...
items.content:
Why inference is becoming more demanding:

Agents don't just respond. They reason, write code, query systems, and iterate.

Every step consumes tokens.

→ Traditional LLM: prompt in, response out
→ Agentic LLM: hundreds of chained reasoning steps per task
→ Each step continuously draws from a token factory

As @HPE and @nvidia help enterprises prepare for these workloads, the CPU is becoming an increasingly important consideration alongside the GPU.

items.title: The edge-to-cloud continuum is the connected path where some decisions occur close to the device, wh...
items.content:
The edge-to-cloud continuum is the connected path where some decisions occur close to the device, while others move to the cloud for broader analysis.

Data that needs a fast response can stay near the source, while the cloud supports coordination and scale.

Microblog @antgrasso

Think of a sensor in a factory.

If it detects a machine problem, waiting for every signal to travel to the cloud may be too slow.

Processing data locally can trigger a faster response, reduce network traffic, and keep operations running even when connectivity is limited.

The same logic applies to a smart vehicle, a hospital device, or a retail store.

Some signals need immediate local action because timing matters.

Other data can move to the cloud, where it can be compared across locations, stored for longer periods, and used to improve future decisions.

This balance helps organizations build systems that react quickly when needed and still remain connected at scale.

Edge-to-cloud works best when companies design systems around which data needs immediate local action and which data should move to the cloud for wider coordination.

items.content:
I built an AI employee to do a big part of my job from Slack.

I consult for companies and teach a machine learning cohort, but I spend most of my time doing boring administrative work.

I've never hired anyone because I don't want to deal with employees.

For years, I've been automating some of the things I do. That's been going great, but there are things that I can't write scripts for.

So I started using an AI Employee on Slack from @viktor__com to deal with my less structured tasks:

1. It reads threads in the cohort channels
2. It drafts responses
3. It flags questions that keep coming back
4. It proposes places in the materials that I should fix
5. It gives me lists of things I need to handle

I make every final decision. Nothing ships without me looking at it first.

Something promising about these AI employees: they get better over time. They are always on the latest model, but most importantly, they learn from your interactions with them.

Viktor is awesome. They were gracious enough to give $100 in credits to everyone who tries them using the link below.

↓

items.content:
@TedwardHall @_whitneywebb When I started my blog in 2000 I had no idea it would eventually be fed into an AI. 

Grok already can tell you about all that about me. It knows my credit score and more. 

I don't know if I ever made an informed choice to participate in this world. But here we are and I'm rolling with it. 

Being a public figure gives me many advantages over those who are desperately trying to hold onto their privacy. 

And I can never go back to the privacy world. Once you become publicly known no going back. 

In the next 20 years we will see many brain/computer interfaces that can figure out what you are thinking. The last bastion of privacy is your inner thoughts. 

Give that up and you get super powers. 

So we all will, just watch.

items.summary_html: Mollick posts GLSL shader source code for an infinite drowned neo-gothic city scene.
items.content_html:
precision highp float;

uniform vec2 resolution;

uniform vec2 mouse;

uniform float time;

out vec4 outColor;

// ----------------------------------------------------------------

// DROWNED SPIRES v2 - infinite neo-gothic city in a stormy ocean

// https://t.co/oirnILHfXn : classic (300 es)

// ----------------------------------------------------------------

float hash11(float p){ p = fract(p*0.1031); p *= p + 33.33; p *= p + p; return fract(p); }

float hash12(vec2 p){ vec3 p3 = fract(vec3(p.xyx)*0.1031); p3 += dot(p3, p3.yzx + 33.33); return fract((p3.x + p3.y)*p3.z); }

float vnoise(vec2 p){

vec2 i = floor(p), f = fract(p);

vec2 u = f*f*(3.0 - 2.0*f);

return mix(mix(hash12(i), hash12(i + vec2(1,0)), u.x),

mix(hash12(i + vec2(0,1)), hash12(i + vec2(1,1)), u.x), u.y);

}

float fbm(vec2 p){

float s = 0.0, a = 0.5;

for(int i = 0; i < 5; i++){ s += a*vnoise(p); p = p*2.03 + vec2(19.7, 7.3); a *= 0.5; }

return s;

}

float fbm3(vec2 p){

float s = 0.0, a = 0.5;

for(int i = 0; i < 3; i++){ s += a*vnoise(p); p = p*2.11 + vec2(9.2, 3.7); a *= 0.5; }

return s;

}

float sdBox(vec3 p, vec3 b){

vec3 d = abs(p) - b;

return length(max(d, 0.0)) + min(max(d.x, max(d.y, d.z)), 0.0);

}

float sdRBox(vec3 p, vec3 b, float r){ return sdBox(p, b) - r; }

// capped cone, centered, y in [-h,h], radius r1 at bottom, r2 at top

float sdCappedCone(vec3 p, float h, float r1, float r2){

vec2 q = vec2(length(p.xz), p.y);

vec2 k1 = vec2(r2, h);

vec2 k2 = vec2(r2 - r1, 2.0*h);

vec2 ca = vec2(q.x - min(q.x, (q.y < 0.0) ? r1 : r2), abs(q.y) - h);

vec2 cb = q - k1 + k2*clamp(dot(k1 - q, k2)/dot(k2, k2), 0.0, 1.0);

float s = (cb.x < 0.0 && ca.y < 0.0) ? -1.0 : 1.0;

return s*sqrt(min(dot(ca,ca), dot(cb,cb)));

}

// ---------------- the city ----------------

const float CELL = 9.0;

bool isBlvd(vec2 id){ return abs(id.x*CELL + CELL*0.5) < 8.0; }

float towerH(vec2 id){

float H = mix(-4.0, 34.0, pow(hash12(id), 1.6));

if(isBlvd(id)) H = min(H, mix(-4.0, 3.0, hash12(id + 5.77))); // drowned boulevard

return max(H, 0.5);

}

float towers(vec3 p){

vec2 id = floor(p.xz/CELL);

vec3 q = p; q.xz = mod(p.xz, CELL) - CELL*0.5;

float H = towerH(id);

float W = 1.3 + 1.1*hash12(id + 17.31);

float R = hash12(id + 41.70);

vec3 aq = vec3(abs(q.x), q.y, abs(q.z));

// main shaft

float d = sdRBox(q - vec3(0.0, H*0.5, 0.0), vec3(W, H*0.5, W), 0.07);

// setback tier

float tierH = H*0.25 + 1.5;

d = min(d, sdRBox(q - vec3(0.0, H + tierH*0.5, 0.0), vec3(W*0.72, tierH*0.5, W*0.72), 0.06));

// spire

float spH = (4.0 + 4.0*R + W*1.5) * (isBlvd(id) ? 0.55 : 1.0);

d = min(d, sdCappedCone(q - vec3(0.0, H + tierH + spH*0.5, 0.0), spH*0.5, W*0.62, 0.03));

// corner pinnacles

d = min(d, sdCappedCone(aq - vec3(W*0.88, H + 1.6, W*0.88), 1.6, 0.42, 0.03));

// buttress fins

d = min(d, sdRBox(aq - vec3(W + 0.10, H*0.42, 0.0), vec3(0.30, H*0.42, 0.55), 0.05));

d = min(d, sdRBox(aq - vec3(0.0, H*0.42, W + 0.10), vec3(0.55, H*0.42, 0.30), 0.05));

return d;

}

// ---------------- the ocean ----------------

float waveH(vec2 p, float t){

float w1 = p.x*0.140 + p.y*0.090 + t*0.85 + 0.9*sin( p.x*0.070 - p.y*0.110 + t*0.50);

float w2 = -p.x*0.210 + p.y*0.170 + t*1.30 + 1.9 + 0.8*sin( p.x*0.110 + p.y*0.060 - t*0.42);

float h = 0.0;

h += 1.25*sin(w1);

h += 1.15*sin(w2);

h += 0.55*sin( p.x*0.340 - p.y*0.260 + t*1.90 + 4.0);

h += 0.30*sin( p.x*0.590 + p.y*0.500 + t*2.70 + 2.0);

h += 0.55*pow(max(h*0.32, 0.0), 2.0); // sharpen the crests

return h;

}

vec2 map(vec3 p){

float dt = towers(p);

float dw = (p.y - waveH(p.xz, time))*0.50;

return (dt < dw) ? vec2(dt, 1.0) : vec2(dw, 2.0);

}

vec2 raycast(vec3 ro, vec3 rd){

float t = 0.0, m = -1.0;

for(int i = 0; i < 160; i++){

vec2 h = map(ro + rd*t);

if(h.x < 0.0012*t + 0.0008){ m = h.y; break; }

t += h.x*0.8;

if(t > 240.0) break;

}

if(t > 240.0) m = -1.0;

return vec2(t, m);

}

float marchTowers(vec3 ro, vec3 rd){

float t = 0.0;

for(int i = 0; i < 48; i++){

float d = towers(ro + rd*t);

if(d < 0.03 + 0.001*t) return t;

t += d*0.9;

if(t > 120.0) break;

}

return -1.0;

}

vec3 towerNormal(vec3 p){

const vec2 e = vec2(0.002, -0.002);

return normalize(e.xyy*towers(p + e.xyy) + e.yyx*towers(p + e.yyx) +

e.yxy*towers(p + e.yxy) + https://t.co/6lZjGExq0y*towers(p + https://t.co/6lZjGExq0y));

}

vec3 waterNormal(vec3 p, float t){

vec2 e = vec2(0.07, 0.0);

float h = waveH(p.xz, t);

vec3 n = normalize(vec3(h - waveH(p.xz + e.xy, t), e.x, h - waveH(p.xz + e.yx, t)));

// choppy detail

vec2 bp = p.xz*2.4 + vec2(t*1.1, t*0.7);

float b0 = fbm3(bp);

n += vec3((b0 - fbm3(bp + vec2(0.14, 0.0)))*1.6, 0.0,

(b0 - fbm3(bp + vec2(0.0, 0.14)))*1.6);

// fine sparkle ripple

vec2 fp = p.xz*6.0 - vec2(t*2.2, t*1.4);

float f0 = vnoise(fp);

n += vec3(f0 - vnoise(fp + vec2(0.20, 0.0)), 0.0,

f0 - vnoise(fp + vec2(0.0, 0.20)))*0.9;

return normalize(n);

}

// ---------------- lightning bolt ----------------

float bolt(vec3 rd, float flash){

float fid = floor(time*0.5);

float fp = fract(time*0.5);

float amp = step(0.70, hash11(fid*1.618))*exp(-3.0*fp);

if(amp < 0.05 || rd.y < 0.015) return 0.0;

vec2 sp = rd.xz/(rd.y + 0.18);

float x0 = (hash11(fid + 51.0) - 0.5)*1.2;

float px = x0, py = 1.05;

float dist = 1e3;

for(int i = 0; i < 10; i++){

float fi = float(i);

float jr = hash11(fid*3.1 + fi*17.7);

float nx = px + (jr - 0.5)*(0.50 + 0.35*fi/9.0);

float ny = 1.05 + (fi + 1.0)*0.34;

vec2 a = vec2(px, py), ba = vec2(nx - px, ny - py);

vec2 pa = sp - a;

float hseg = clamp(dot(pa, ba)/dot(ba, ba), 0.0, 1.0);

dist = min(dist, length(pa - ba*hseg));

px = nx; py = ny;

}

return amp*(exp(-dist*95.0)*5.0 + exp(-dist*12.0)*0.18);

}

// ---------------- stormy sky ----------------

vec3 sky(vec3 rd, float flash, vec3 fdir){

float t = time;

float y = max(rd.y, 0.0);

vec3 col = mix(vec3(0.088, 0.100, 0.112), vec3(0.008, 0.014, 0.028), pow(y, 0.40));

vec2 sc = rd.xz/(y + 0.14);

float c1 = fbm (sc*0.55 + vec2(t*0.030, t*0.018));

float c2 = fbm3(sc*1.40 - vec2(t*0.055, t*0.010));

float cov = smoothstep(0.35, 0.66, c1*0.72 + c2*0.42);

vec3 cloudCol = mix(vec3(0.026, 0.033, 0.046), vec3(0.130, 0.140, 0.155), c2);

col = mix(col, cloudCol, cov*smoothstep(-0.02, 0.22, y));

// pale moon behind the clouds

vec3 md = normalize(vec3(0.40, 0.42, -0.55));

float dm = max(dot(rd, md), 0.0);

col += vec3(0.30, 0.35, 0.42)*pow(dm, 60.0)*(1.0 - cov)*0.9;

col += vec3(0.045, 0.055, 0.075)*pow(dm, 5.0);

// lightning glow + bolt

float lf = pow(max(dot(rd, fdir), 0.0), 6.0);

col += flash*(vec3(0.10, 0.12, 0.20) + vec3(0.55, 0.60, 0.75)*lf)*(1.0 + cov*1.5);

col += vec3(0.72, 0.78, 1.00)*bolt(rd, flash);

return col;

}

// ---------------- gothic windows ----------------

vec2 windows(vec3 p, vec3 n, float H){

vec2 id = floor(p.xz/CELL);

vec3 q = p; q.xz = mod(p.xz, CELL) - CELL*0.5;

float u = (abs(n.x) > abs(n.z)) ? q.z : q.x;

float v = p.y;

vec2 g = vec2(u*0.9, v*0.42);

vec2 gi = floor(g);

vec2 gf = fract(g);

float rnd = hash12(id*7.13 + gi*3.71);

float lit = step(0.48, rnd);

float x = abs(gf.x - 0.5)*2.0;

float y = gf.y;

float w = 0.46;

// lancet window: body + pointed arch

float win = step(x, w)*step(0.10, y)*step(y, 0.62);

win = max(win, step(x, w*(1.0 - (y - 0.62)/0.23))*step(0.62, y)*step(y, 0.85));

win *= step(2.2, v)*step(v, H)*step(abs(n.y), 0.5);

return vec2(win*lit, rnd);

}

vec3 shadeTower(vec3 p, vec3 n, vec3 rd, float flash, vec3 fdir){

vec2 id = floor(p.xz/CELL);

float H = towerH(id);

float tone = 0.7 + 0.6*hash12(id + 3.1);

vec3 alb = vec3(0.052, 0.055, 0.068)*tone;

// vertical stone ribs, pitched with the window grid

vec3 q = p; q.xz = mod(p.xz, CELL) - CELL*0.5;

float u = (abs(n.x) > abs(n.z)) ? q.z : q.x;

float rib = 0.82 + 0.18*smoothstep(-0.3, 0.9, cos(u*5.655));

alb *= mix(1.0, rib, step(abs(n.y), 0.5));

float ao = clamp(p.y*0.10 + 0.30, 0.0, 1.0);

float wet = 1.0 - smoothstep(1.2, 4.5, p.y);

alb *= 1.0 - 0.55*wet;

vec3 col = alb*(0.45 + 0.55*ao)*(0.65 + 0.35*clamp(n.y, 0.0, 1.0));

// dim moonlight so facades keep their form between flashes

vec3 md = normalize(vec3(0.40, 0.42, -0.55));

col += alb*vec3(0.28, 0.34, 0.44)*max(dot(n, md), 0.0)*0.8;

// lightning key light

vec3 key = vec3(0.72, 0.80, 1.00);

col += alb*key*max(dot(n, fdir), 0.0)*(0.06 + 3.5*flash);

// wet sheen

vec3 rr = reflect(rd, n);

col += key*pow(max(dot(rr, fdir), 0.0), 32.0)*(0.10 + 0.60*wet)*(0.05 + 2.5*flash);

// sky rim

col += alb*vec3(0.30, 0.40, 0.50)*pow(1.0 - max(dot(-rd, n), 0.0), 4.0)*0.4;

// windows

vec2 win = windows(p, n, H);

float flk = 0.65 + 0.35*sin(time*2.2 + win.y*40.0);

vec3 wcol = mix(vec3(1.0, 0.60, 0.25), vec3(0.45, 0.70, 1.0), step(0.90, win.y));

col += wcol*win.x*1.30*flk*(0.35 + 1.15*fract(win.y*17.77));

return col;

}

vec3 shadeWater(vec3 p, vec3 rd, float flash, vec3 fdir){

vec3 n = waterNormal(p, time);

vec3 rrd = reflect(rd, n);

rrd.y = abs(rrd.y) + 0.02;

vec3 refl = sky(rrd, flash, fdir);

// dark tower reflections

vec3 rro = p + n*0.08;

float rt = marchTowers(rro, rrd);

if(rt > 0.0) refl = mix(vec3(0.010, 0.014, 0.022), refl, 1.0 - exp(-rt*0.05));

float fres = 0.02 + 0.98*pow(1.0 - max(dot(-rd, n), 0.0), 5.0);

float wh = waveH(p.xz, time);

float crest = smoothstep(1.5, 2.8, wh);

vec3 deep = vec3(0.005, 0.020, 0.026)*(0.55 + 0.45*smoothstep(-2.0, 2.0, wh));

deep += vec3(0.006, 0.045, 0.045)*crest;

deep += vec3(0.06, 0.07, 0.09)*flash*crest;

vec3 col = mix(deep, refl*0.85, fres);

// moon glitter

vec3 md = normalize(vec3(0.40, 0.42, -0.55));

vec3 hv2 = normalize(md - rd);

col += vec3(0.50, 0.55, 0.60)*pow(max(dot(n, hv2), 0.0), 260.0)*0.12;

// lightning specular

vec3 hv = normalize(fdir - rd);

col += vec3(0.8, 0.85, 1.0)*pow(max(dot(n, hv), 0.0), 220.0)*flash*2.0;

// foam: wave crests + around tower bases

float dT = towers(p);

float nearT = 1.0 - smoothstep(0.15, 1.6, dT);

float nz = fbm3(p.xz*2.2 + vec2(time*0.40, -time*0.30));

float foam = max(smoothstep(1.9, 3.0, wh)*0.9, nearT)

* smoothstep(0.45, 0.78, nz);

vec3 foamCol = vec3(0.34, 0.38, 0.40)*(0.30 + 1.3*flash + 0.15*crest);

col = mix(col, foamCol, clamp(foam, 0.0, 1.0)*0.8);

// warm window-light shimmering on the swell near the towers

float shim = smoothstep(0.45, 0.85, fbm3(p.xz*3.1 + vec2(time*1.2, -time*0.8)));

col += vec3(1.0, 0.55, 0.22)*(1.0 - smoothstep(0.5, 3.5, dT))*shim*0.09;

return col;

}

void main(){

vec2 fc = gl_FragCoord.xy;

vec2 uv = (fc*2.0 - resolution)/resolution.y;

// lightning timing

float ft = time*0.5;

float fid = floor(ft), fp = fract(ft);

float gate = step(0.70, hash11(fid*1.618));

float flash = gate*exp(-4.5*fp)*(0.55 + 0.45*sin(fp*85.0 + hash11(fid + 2.0)*6.283));

vec3 fdir = normalize(vec3(hash11(fid + 11.0) - 0.5,

0.30 + 0.35*hash11(fid + 23.0),

hash11(fid + 37.0) - 0.5));

// camera drifting down the drowned boulevard

float T = time;

vec3 ro = vec3(sin(T*0.11)*1.2, 5.5 + sin(T*0.55)*0.3, T*5.0);

ro.y += waveH(ro.xz, T)*0.22;

vec3 fw = normalize(vec3(sin(T*0.11 + 0.6)*0.35, -0.13 + sin(T*0.23)*0.03, 1.0));

vec2 mo = (mouse - 0.5)*2.0;

if(mouse.x == 0.0 && mouse.y == 0.0) mo = vec2(0.0);

float ca = cos(mo.x*0.5), sa = sin(mo.x*0.5);

fw = vec3(fw.x*ca + fw.z*sa, fw.y - mo.y*0.3, -fw.x*sa + fw.z*ca);

fw = normalize(fw);

vec3 ri = normalize(cross(fw, vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)));

vec3 up = cross(ri, fw);

float rl = sin(T*0.15)*0.035 + mo.x*0.05;

vec3 rr2 = ri*cos(rl) + up*sin(rl);

vec3 uu = up*cos(rl) - ri*sin(rl);

vec3 rd = normalize(fw*1.5 + rr2*uv.x + uu*uv.y);

// march

vec2 hit = raycast(ro, rd);

vec3 col;

if(hit.y < 0.0){

col = sky(rd, flash, fdir);

} else {

vec3 p = ro + rd*hit.x;

col = (hit.y < 1.5) ? shadeTower(p, towerNormal(p), rd, flash, fdir)

: shadeWater(p, rd, flash, fdir);

// mist band hugging the sea

float mist = (1.0 - exp(-hit.x*0.045))*exp(-max(p.y, 0.0)*0.20);

col = mix(col, vec3(0.075, 0.088, 0.105)*(0.7 + 0.9*flash), mist*0.42);

float fog = 1.0 - exp(-hit.x*0.010);

col = mix(col, sky(normalize(vec3(rd.x, 0.03, rd.z)), flash, fdir), fog);

}

// rain streaks

float rn = hash12(floor(vec2(fc.x*0.30, fc.y*0.05 + time*9.0)));

col += vec3(0.45, 0.52, 0.60)*smoothstep(0.994, 1.0, rn)*0.10;

// filmic-ish tone map + grain + vignette

col *= vec3(0.92, 1.00, 1.10)*0.80;

col = (col*(2.51*col + 0.03))/(col*(2.43*col + 0.59) + 0.14);

col = pow(clamp(col, 0.0, 1.0), vec3(0.4545));

col += (hash12(fc + vec2(fract(time)*761.0, fract(time)*359.0)) - 0.5)*0.028;

vec2 vuv = fc/resolution;

col *= 0.55 + 0.45*pow(16.0*vuv.x*vuv.y*(1.0 - vuv.x)*(1.0 - vuv.y), 0.22);

outColor = vec4(col, 1.0);

}

items.content:
Used Claude Code to connect all my blog posts from starting my nomad travels in 2013 all the way to 2018 from post to post

AI is amazing and finding the red line through lots of pieces of content

I will try connect 2018 (mostly in Korea) to 2020 back in Europe (COVID) later too

It's also great at telling me where there's black spots that have no content and I can write about

I wrote most actively 2013-2015 because everything was new while traveling and then slowly less travel blogs, also travel blogging became less and less popular and many stopped around 2016 as people were getting cancelled left and right for just using the wrong words back then! One of my most famous blogger friends quit then for that reason, sadly

Now is a different time and you can write whatever you want again freely thank god

I still think travel blogging will make a come back, I've been travel blogging a lot on here every time I go somewhere and it's still really fun to write and just as fun to read your experiences years later

Your brain changes and it's fun to see your perspective and personality change through posts

Anyway if you'd like to read this travel blog chain, you can start here https://t.co/5xtZcNgaW0

@TedwardHall If you give up your privacy your agents work better. 

I'm in a completely post-privacy world. Go to Grok and ask it how I think. It knows more about me than I know about myself. 

And now I can use that to simulate a conversation with me and Elon Musk, for instance. 

Or answer my email. 

What a world we are in now, but I don't think even Steve recognized how deeply privacy would go away. And Apple has to keep up with the times, even though it is one of the best at protecting our privacy.

@RealMattMalecki @Flock Yeah. Unless you live in China. :-)

Getting a warrant signed isn't that tough if they have a reason to watch you. 

And most of us aren't worth watching. Most humans are pretty boring. 

And there are plenty of ways to catch people without watching them. 

The guy who runs the satellites to make sure that another Timothy McVeigh doesn't happen tells me he looks for farmers spreading nitrates on the ground. 

And if he finds one that didn't put the nitrate on the ground that he/she bought they go visit them, then they get a warrant to watch the person who did buy it.

items.content:
I see this pattern everywhere.

Companies invest heavily in:

→ Models
→ Data platforms
→ Automation
 
But resilient connectivity is still overlooked.

When connectivity becomes inconsistent, operational visibility and connected workflows can become more difficult to manage.

AI didn’t fail.

The underlying infrastructure became a challenge.
That’s not just an IT issue—it’s an operational resilience issue.

items.content:
Here is what this means for AI strategy specifically.

Your AI models need operational data. Your cloud applications rely on resilient connectivity. Your payments, robotics, analytics, and field operations all depend on connected infrastructure.

When connectivity becomes inconsistent, operational visibility and workflow coordination can become more difficult to manage.

It can slow decision-making and impact how connected systems operate across distributed environments.

The AI may be well designed. The infrastructure may be sophisticated. But resilient network infrastructure is becoming increasingly important for supporting AI-enabled operations.

Let me challenge a belief most IT leaders hold.

“We have a backup ISP. We’re protected.”

But businesses are realizing connectivity resilience can become more complicated across distributed environments.

If multiple connections rely on similar infrastructure dependencies, disruptions can still impact connected operations and workflows.

That’s why more organizations are reevaluating how they approach resilient connectivity infrastructure.

items.content:
Yes I'm starting to believe this too

"Avoid the sun" is like saying "never lift weights" because you might get an injury

But you have to lift weights, it's a non-negotiable for maintaining your health after age 30

So you have lift weights with proper form and weight for your body preferably with a personal trainer, same as sunlight, you have to be in the sun at specific times at specific UV strengths or you will get sunburns, increase your cancer risk, and it just generally being bad for you

During COVID we learnt how important the sun was for due to our collective lack of Vitamin D
